segments.text: YouTube has studied upload timing for years. Its help page says {q}growth in views across uploads is not correlated with time between uploads.
So the algorithm isn't checking your calendar. Posting more still pays off, though.
YouTube judges {f1}each video on its own fresh data. {f2}Who clicks, how long they watch, likes, shares, and {f3}not-interested feedback.
TikTok, in twenty twenty: {t1}the amount of videos you post won't impact how your content is recommended.
Breaks don't hurt either. YouTube {b1}found no correlation between break length and changes in views.
Your audience {b2}may just need time to warm up again.
Buffer tracked over a hundred thousand accounts for {w1}twenty-six weeks.
Those who posted in {w2}at least twenty of them got {w3}four hundred and fifty percent more engagement per post than those who posted in four or fewer.
vidIQ looked at {v1}ten million YouTube channels over a year.
Under {v2}one upload a month, median view growth was zero point five three percent a month. At {v3}twelve or more, two point one eight. {v4}About four times.
vidIQ calls it {c1}correlation, not causation. Bigger channels can afford to post more.
So to an algorithm, consistency means more videos to score. TikTok's feed {r1}generally pulls from the last ninety days.
And YouTube lists {r2}uploading less frequently than usual as one reason recommended traffic drops.
Post as often as you can keep the quality up. Take breaks when you need them, and judge each video on its own numbers.
